title: VCP
teaches: The VCP (volatility contraction pattern) as we trade it: a leader in an uptrend pulls back in a run of swings that each get smaller, volume dries up into the tight final swing, the pivot is the high of that final swing, the buy is the trade through it at market in regular hours and no more than 4% past it, the stop sits a few cents under the entry day's low, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the trail, and a loss at the stop is the system working.

facts.quote: Stop first (by default a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, F62); the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.

facts.quote: The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule (B20).
facts.claim: A4: the stop is the exit; it only moves up, never wider; the gap rule is the one exception.

facts.quote: Shares = account × risk % ÷ (entry − stop), rounded down, then capped: the size is the SMALLER of the risk-based size and the position cap

questions.q: What does a VCP stand for?
choices: Volatility Contraction Pattern
Velocity Confirmation Pattern
Volume Compression Pattern
Volatile Continuation Pattern
questions.why: Volatility Contraction Pattern. The name is about price swings that contract. A sideways wiggle whose contractions do not shrink is not a VCP.
questions.lesson_line: VCP stands for volatility contraction pattern. The swings in the base contract.

wrong.Volume Compression Pattern: Volume matters, but the name is about the size of the price swings.
wrong.Velocity Confirmation Pattern: That is not the name. A VCP is named for price swings that contract.
wrong.Volatile Continuation Pattern: The name says contraction, not continuation. It is named for swings that shrink.

questions.simple: The name is Volatility Contraction Pattern, as the price swings in the base contract more and more.

reasons: the name is quoted from the ChartMill guide; the Minervini archive pages could not be reopened in this pass

questions.q: In a VCP, the price swings get smaller from the left side of the base to the right side.
questions.why: True. Minervini wants greater volatility on the left side of the price base and lesser volatility on the right. Falling volume at points signals a finished base. Swings that do not shrink are not a VCP: calling any sideways wiggle a VCP is a named mistake.
questions.lesson_line: Left side wide, right side tight. The swings contract.
questions.simple: True, because a VCP base moves from wide, loose swings on the left to small, tight swings on the right.

questions.q: What is the pivot of a VCP?
choices: The low of the first pullback
The close before the breakout
The high of the final contraction
The highest price in the base
questions.answer: The high of the final contraction
questions.why: The high of the final contraction. ChartMill: the pivot is the top of the final contraction, not the highest price of the entire base, but the level the final tight consolidation keeps running into. Our rule agrees: it may sit below the base's left-side high.
questions.lesson_line: The pivot is the top of the last, tightest swing.

questions.q: On a VCP breakout, which is our primary stop?
choices: Exactly on the day's low
At the 50-day average
At the low of the first pullback
A few cents under the day's low

questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the day's low, then size from the stop.

wrong.Exactly on the day's low: Our rule is a few cents under the low, not exactly on it.

questions.q: A VCP is a pause inside a prior uptrend, not a base in a downtrend.

questions.lesson_line: The base sits inside an uptrend. A tight base in a downtrend does not qualify.
questions.simple: True. A VCP is a pause inside an uptrend, and Minervini never goes against the long-term trend.

choices: A Stage 2 uptrend
A Stage 4 downtrend
A sideways drift under the 200-day

questions.lesson_line: Red market: no VCP buys. Even perfect bases fail when buyers are missing.

90 or more

questions.lesson_line: We buy leaders: RS 80 or more in a strong group.

questions.lesson_line: No longs under the 200-day. A VCP has to pass that first.
questions.simple: The 200-day average. We do not buy a long that sits below it.

questions.q: Which floor applies to a VCP we buy?

$10 a share and $20 million a day
No floor if the base is tight

+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B23)

questions.q: The first pullback is 24%. Each next one is half the last. How deep is the third?
questions.why: Halve the 24% once for the second pullback, then halve that result for the third, which gives 6%. Minervini likes each contraction to be about half of the one before, give or take. That is a rule of thumb, so real bases land near it, not exactly on it.
questions.lesson_line: About half each time. The swings shrink fast.
questions.simple: Halve the 24 percent once, then halve the result again. That leaves 6 percent for the third pullback.

deeper.example: Minervini's classic progression runs from a 25 percent correction to 10 percent to 5 percent. Those steps are not exact halves. His rule of thumb is about half, give or take. Use half as a guide, not a fixed ratio.

reasons: +2 a computed key
+2 sits beside the held decision D-059 on the contraction ratio
+1 fixed before

questions.why: The depth is the high minus the low, divided by the high: (170.00 minus 164.05) divided by 170.00 is 3.5%. ChartMill wants the final contraction under 10%, and 3% to 6% is best. Our card says 10% or less.
questions.lesson_line: Depth is high minus low, divided by the high. The last swing should be the tightest.

questions.lesson_line: Measure the stop in percent before you size the trade.

+2 sits beside the held decision D-005 on stop width

questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open. It is a yardstick, and the first sell is a judgment.

questions.why: The chase limit is the pivot plus 4%. Multiply the pivot by 1.04: 16.47 times 1.04 is 17.13 to the nearest cent. We never buy more than 4% above the buy point. Past that, the stop stays put, the distance grows and the shares shrink.
questions.lesson_line: Know the chase limit before the open: 4% over the pivot.
questions.simple: Add 4 percent to the pivot. 16.47 times 1.04 is about 17.13, the chase limit.

reasons: +2 a computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C28)

wrong.$16.54: That adds a fraction of a percent, not 4 percent. A decimal slip.
wrong.$15.81: That takes 4% off. The chase limit sits above the pivot.

questions.q: What is your move?
choices: Buy half now and the rest on a dip
Buy it now; the volume is heavy
Pass; more than 4% past the pivot
Buy fewer shares; the risk is the same

wrong.Buy half now and the rest on a dip: We do not scale in. One full buy, one stop.

questions.q: In a VCP the final contraction should be the tightest swing of the base.
questions.why: True. Contractions shrink from left to right, so the final one is the smallest. ChartMill calls it the most important contraction: ideally under 10%, best at 3% to 6%. Our rule allows 10% or less.
questions.lesson_line: The last swing is the tightest, and it sets the pivot.
questions.simple: True, because the swings shrink toward the right, so the last one is the tightest and should be 10% or less.

reasons: final contraction at most 10% is a proposed card criterion

questions.q: How should volume look in the final contraction?
choices: Spiking on a wide, heavy down day
Drying up, below the 50-day average
Rising, above the 50-day average
About the same as in the first swing
questions.why: Drying up, below the 50-day average. Our rule wants the final contraction's average daily volume below the first contraction's and below the 50-day average, with at least one day at or under half the 50-day average. Volume at or above the average is not a dry-up. This tests the last swing, not the breakout day.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet price, quiet volume. Volume dries up into the tight final swing.

wrong.Rising, above the 50-day average: Volume above the 50-day average is not a dry-up. Our rule wants it below.
wrong.Spiking on a wide, heavy down day: That is a heavy down day. It ends the setup before the buy.
wrong.About the same as in the first swing: The final swing's volume should be below the first swing's, not equal to it.

volume_dry is a proposed criterion

questions.q: Is this base contracting?
choices: No; the swings do not shrink
Yes; three pullbacks make a VCP
Yes; the dips are shallow
No; the first dip is too small

questions.lesson_line: Equal swings are a box, not a VCP. Wait for the contractions.

wrong.Yes; the dips are shallow: Depth is not the test here. The pullbacks have to shrink, and these do not.
wrong.No; the first dip is too small: A 14% first dip is inside the 10% to 40% range. The problem is that nothing shrinks.

questions.simple: No, because each pullback is as deep as the one before, so nothing is shrinking.

reasons: wide-and-loose invalidation is a proposed card criterion

questions.q: Which setup is this?
choices: A VCP
A flat base
A high tight flag
A cup with handle

This one rests six weeks after a 40% run. A VCP's pullbacks shrink one after another, and this box has none that do.
questions.lesson_line: Same-size swings are a box. Shrinking swings are a VCP.

wrong.A VCP: A VCP needs successive pullbacks that shrink. These do not.
wrong.A high tight flag: A high tight flag follows a run of 90% or more in 8 weeks or less. This run was 40% over four months.
wrong.A cup with handle: A cup is one rounded decline and one handle at the rim. This is a flat box.

choices: Base B; its pullbacks get smaller
Base A; one deep pullback is enough
Both; each pulls back and recovers
Neither; a VCP needs a cup shape first

Pass; the base has broken
Buy; it cleared the pivot
Wait a day and buy at the open

Sell it all at tomorrow's open
Hold; the stop is the exit
Widen the stop to give it room

wrong.Add more; it is cheaper: We never add. One full buy, one stop.
wrong.Sell it all at tomorrow's open: A warning is not an exit. The stop decides.
wrong.Widen the stop to give it room: The stop only moves up, never wider. Widening it to give the stock room is a named mistake.

A textbook VCP
